Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failure stems from the way the BrentSolver.solve method handles the case when either endpoint of the bracket interval (min or max) is a root of the function. According to the current bug report, if min or max is a root, the function returns yMin or yMax instead of returning the corresponding min or max point. 

Looking closely at the code snippet of the method BrentSolver.solve(UnivariateRealFunction f, double min, double max, double initial), the relevant parts are:

- Lines 113-116: 
  When the function value at min (yMin) is within the functionValueAccuracy threshold (meaning it is considered a root), the solver performs setResult(yMin, 0) and returns result. This is incorrect because setResult is supposed to be called with the root estimate (the x-axis value), not the function value at that point. Here, yMin is the function value (close to 0), but what should be stored and returned is min, the point on x-axis. The same pattern is seen for max at lines 125-128.

- setResult (double newResult, int iterationCount) at lines 140-144 sets the result field to newResult directly. Since yMin or yMax is the function value, storing yMin or yMax as the root estimate is wrong.

- The rest of the solve method correctly proceeds to bracket the root and call the private solve(f, x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2) method for the main Brent algorithm root finding once it confirms a proper bracket.

- The private solve method (lines 223-318) implements the Brent root-finding logic and returns the correct root x1 found on the interval.

- The test case expects the solver to return Math.PI when the interval's endpoint is Math.PI, which is indeed a root for the SinFunction, but because of the bug, the solver returns yMin or yMax (the function value) instead of min or max (the root), leading to test failure.

Hence, the root cause is the incorrect usage of setResult with function values yMin or yMax in place of the corresponding x-values min or max when the function value is sufficiently close to zero at the endpoints. This results in the solver returning the function root value (approximately 0) instead of the root location (x value).

Recent bug reports do not seem directly relevant to this exact issue, they focus on other aspects of the Brent solver behavior.

Summary:
- In BrentSolver.solve, the lines that check if min or max endpoints are roots call setResult(yMin, 0) and setResult(yMax, 0), which store function values instead of root estimates.
- This causes the solver to return the function value at the root instead of the root itself.
- The fix is to call setResult(min, 0) or setResult(max, 0) respectively instead of setResult(yMin, 0) or setResult(yMax, 0).

This diagnosis explains why the test fails and clarifies how the incorrect handling of root endpoints causes the wrong return values.
The bug occurs because in the method BrentSolver.solve(UnivariateRealFunction f, double min, double max, double initial), the code incorrectly calls setResult(yMin, 0) and setResult(yMax, 0) when the function values at the endpoints min or max are sufficiently close to zero, respectively. Here yMin and yMax are function values, not root estimates. The setResult method stores the result as the root found, so passing the function value instead of the root x-value causes the solver to return the incorrect value (function value close to zero instead of the root location). The test expects the solver to return the root, e.g. Math.PI, when the endpoint is a root. The rest of the solver logic and private solve method correctly find and return roots in other cases. The issue is specifically in the endpoint root checks returning wrong values by passing yMin/yMax instead of min/max to setResult. Fixing those calls to setResult(min, 0) and setResult(max, 0) will correct the behavior and ensure the solver returns the root x-value when an endpoint is root. Recent reports are unrelated to this specific issue.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
